rulings.Rulings: [Part 3 of 3] The Motion to compel further responses to RFPs 15-24, seeking documents related to Decedent Chung Hop Wong's personal tax returns and documents related to his personal taxes, is GRANTED IN PART AND DENIED IN PART. In addition to various objections, among them assertions of privilege, Respondent Kathryn Wong stated as to responsive documents, "None in possession." If Respondent is unable to comply with these RFPs after diligent search and reasonable inquiry, Respondent shall provide a statement in compliance with Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.230 within 30 days of entry of this Order. To the extent there are responsive documents, Respondent shall provide a privilege log within 30 days of entry of this Order (Code of Civil Procedure sec. 2031.240). The Motion to compel further responses to RFPs 25-26 and RFPs 27-34, seeking documents related to Kam's Restaurant's tax returns and sales tax audit(s), is GRANTED. To the extend there are responsive documents, Respondent shall provide a privilege log within 30 days of entry of this Order (Code of Civil Procedure sec. 2031.240). Production of responsive non-privileged documents shall otherwise be subject to the Protective Order set forth as Exhibit A to the Motion, and shall occur within 45 days from the entry of this Order. The Motion to compel further responses to RFP 30 is DENIED, on grounds that, at this time, there is insufficient information offered to the Court to determine how the requested documents may lead to admissible evidence in this case. The Motion to compel further response to RFP 35 is GRANTED, with the modification of the responsive time period to "September 1, 2009 to present." Both parties request monetary sanctions for attorney's fees and costs against the other in this Motion. Sanctions are awarded pursuant to Code of Civil Procedure sections 2030.300(d), 2023.010(a), 2023.010(h), and 2031.310(h). The court finds that neither party made the requisite showing to award reasonable attorney's fees and costs in this Motion. The competing requests for a sanctions award are both DENIED. rulings.Case Title: IN THE MATTER OF THE CHUNG HOP WONG AND KING TSUI LAU WONG REVOCABL TRUST dated sep 21, 2009 amended Sep 26 2009
rulings.Calendar Matter: Petitioners Motion To Compel Respondent Kathryn Wong To Produce Further Responses Pursuant To Requests For Production Of Documents, Set Three
rulings.Rulings: [Part 1 of 3] This tentative ruling is issued by Judge Michael B. McNaughton. Before the court is Petitioners Helen Wong-Joe, Jessica Wong, and Brandon Wong's Motion to Compel Respondent Kathryn Wong to Produce Further Responses Pursuant to Requests for Production of Documents, Set Three, brought pursuant to California Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.310. Per the Notice of Motion, Movants seek an order compelling further responses from Respondent Kathryn Wong to Requests for Production of Documents ("RFPs"), Set Three, No. 1-35; and a privilege log. The Motion also seeks the court's approval of a "Stipulated Protective Order Regarding Confidentiality of Tax-Related Documents" and monetary sanctions. Petitioners propounded Requests for Production of Documents, Set Three on January 15, 2024. On April 23, 2026, Respondent Kathryn served responses consisting only of various objections. Per the Motion's Separate Statement, Petitioners seek further responses to the following categories of documents: RFPs 1-6 and 7-14 seek documents related to Katheryn Wong's personal financial and tax information. RFPs 15-24 seek documents related to Decedent Chung Hop Wong's personal tax information and documents related to his taxes. RFPs 25-26 seek documents related to Kam's Restaurant's tax returns. RFPs 27-34 seek documents related to sale tax audit(s) of Kam's Restaurant. RFP 30 seeks documents related to a Loan Number 2000090580, allegedly secured by 372-374 6th Avenue, San Francisco, CA. RFP 35 seeks documents related to any loan(s) Decedent Chung Hop Wong obtained, secured by 372-374 6th Avenue, San Francisco, CA. The Motion is GRANTED IN PART and DENIED IN PART as follows. A propounding party may move for a motion to compel a further response to an inspection demand and has the initial burden to set forth specific facts showing "good cause" justifying the discovery sought by the inspection demand. (Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.310(a) and (b)(1); Kirkland v. Sup. Ct. (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 92, 98.) That burden is met by a fact-specific showing of relevance, unless there is a legitimate privilege issue or claim of attorney work product, in which case the burden requires more than a mere showing of relevance. (TBG Ins. Services Corp. v. Sup. Ct. (2002) 96 Cal.App.4th 443, 448.) Overall, the Motion does not make a fact-specific showing that the categories of documents sought are narrowly tailored to lead to the discovery of admissible evidence in this case. The court finds the RFPs, as currently propounded, are overbroad in time and scope, based on the allegations made in the underlying Petition. (See, Code of Civ. Proc. section 2017.010.) Further, there are legitimate privilege issues raised by the types of documents and information sought. The Requests for Production of Documents seek "all" personal and business tax documents and information from Respondent, Decedent, and the business allegedly held by the Trust and run by Respondent and settlors. Although the privilege is not absolute, taxpayers - both individuals and corporations - are privileged to withhold disclosure of copies of their state and federal tax returns and the information contained therein (see, Webb v. Standard Oil Co. of California (1957) 49 Cal.2d. 509, 513-514; Sav-On Drugs, Inc. v. Sup Ct. (Botney) (1975) 15 Cal.3d 1.)

rulings.Rulings: [Part 2 of 3] The Motion argues privilege over all the tax returns has been waived because the public policy interest overrides the confidentiality of the tax returns, citing Schnabel v. Sup. Ct. (1993) 5 Cal.4th 704, 721. As discussed in Schnabel, while the public policy exception has been applied in various contexts, the exception is narrowly construed and has been applied only when warranted by legislatively declared public policy. (Ibid.) The Motion offers no legislative declaration asserting the public policy exception over disclosure of tax returns in a breach of trust or trust enforcement action. In addition to the requests for tax returns and related information, the RFPs also seek confidential information and communications related to the tax returns, and all loan application documents, promissory notes, deeds of trust, mortgage statements, underwriting files, closing statements, payment histories, and communications relating to Loan Number 2000090580 secured by 372-374 6th Avenue, "from inception through the present." These types of documents carry their own privilege and privacy protections, which must be overcome by the party seeking them. Financial information is a constitutional "zone of privacy" recognized in case law. "[T]here is a right to privacy in confidential customer information whatever form it takes, whether that form be tax returns, checks, statements, or other account information." (Fortunato v. Sup.Ct. (Ingrassia) (2003) 114 Cal.4th 475, 481, emphasis in original. See also, e.g., Cobb v. Sup.Ct. (Tleel) (1979) 99 Cal.3d 543, 550.) However, that protection in the context of discovery is qualified, not absolute. If the party seeking the discovery has shown the confidential information is directly relevant to a cause of action (a higher standard than baseline "relevancy"), the court must balance the claimed right of privacy versus the public interest in civil litigants access to relevant facts. (Valley Bank of Nevada v. Sup.Ct. (Barkett) (1975) 15 Cal.3d 652, 657.) In balancing a person's privacy interest versus a litigant's interest in relevant facts, the court must consider, at least: the purpose of the information sought; the effect disclosure will have on the parties and the trial; the nature of the withholding party's objections; and the "ability of the court to make an alternative order which may grant partial disclosure, disclosure in another form, or disclosure only in the event that the party seeking the information undertakes certain specified burdens which appear just under the circumstances." (Valley Bank of Nevada v. Sup.Ct. (Barkett), supra, 15 Cal.3d at 658; see Pioneer Electronics (USA), Inc. v. Sup.Ct. (Olmstead) (2007) 40 Cal.4th 360, 371.) The Motion to compel further responses to RFPs 1-6 and 7-14 is DENIED, for the reasons stated above regarding the Motion's deficient showing of "good cause" and the protections afforded personal financial and tax information. The requests are overbroad as to scope and timeframe. The Motion has not shown how the confidential consumer information contained in the documents sought is narrowly tailored to lead to discover admissible evidence. Even if the court were to find that Petitioners had met that threshold showing, the court does not find that the Motion sufficiently supports a finding that the Respondent's privacy interests are outweighed by the Petitioners' interest in that private information, based on the allegations made on face of the underlying Petition. The nature of Respondent's objections, and the Motion's insufficient showing of good cause to order production of the subject categories of information, leaves the court unable to craft an alternative order granting partial disclosure or disclosure in another form, on the record currently before it on this Motion.
